extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers; coffee-house public interested in literature, theatre, and current affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Short-periodical essays and coffee-house criticism evaluating poetry, epic diction, theatre, acting, and what counts as 'news' for a cultivated readership. Mix of literary criticism and theatrical taste-making directed at readers of a periodical (The Tatler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness = gives new knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: 'we generally spend the evening at this table in inquiries into antiquity, and think anything news which gives us new knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as 'news' only what provides new knowledge or instructive information; preference for items that illuminate antiquity or new learning. (Implicit example: turning Homeric action into an 'exact journal' as a form of newsworthy inquiry.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious use of epithets in epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Virgil is more judicious than the other in the epithets he gives his hero.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer epithets that fit the character and action; avoid overuse or mechanical repetition of stock epithets. The critic tests a poet by searching for moments where habitual epithets would be absurd and praises poets who drop inappropriate labels (example: Virgil dropping 'pius' or 'pater' where they would be incongruous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epithets inconsistent with depicted action
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Homer: mentioning nimbleness of foot in Achilles though he is 'standing, sitting, lying down, fighting, eating, drinking' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anti-pattern is employing a fixed epithet (e.g., 'swift-footed') at every mention regardless of context; good diction aligns description with the immediate activity or posture of the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character descriptions must accord with moral epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that a 'loose action might be consistent enough with the usual manners of a soldier, though it became neither the chastity of a pious man, nor the gravity of the father of a people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying high moral or familial epithets (e.g., 'pious', 'father of a people'), ensure the depicted actions do not contradict those qualities; avoid jarring moral incoherence between trait-labels and behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage presentation of noble characters to improve public taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Eugenio: 'The amendment of these low gratifications is only to be made by people of condition, by encouraging the presentation of the noble characters drawn by Shakespeare and others, from whence it is impossible to return without strong impressions of honour and humanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers, patrons, and audiences of theatre should favor plays that present elevated, noble characters because such representation instills honour and humanity in spectators; this is an aesthetic and moral prescription for repertoire selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical content that offends reason or shame
rubrics_metrics.description: Players 'are obliged to repeat and assume proper gestures for representing things, of which their reason must be ashamed, and which they must disdain their audience for approving.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an anti-pattern, repertoire that forces actors into shameful or obscene representations should be curtailed; theatre should not normalize actions that reason and moral sensibility would condemn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit theatre's unique power to shape emotion and character
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If a thing painted or related can irresistibly enter our hearts, what may not be brought to pass by seeing generous things performed before our eyes?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stagecraft (person, manner, look, motion) has a stronger formative effect than painting or history alone; thus great poets and accomplished players can profoundly move and educate audiences—use theatre deliberately for moral and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and actor pairing influence performance quality
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Skilful actors think it a very peculiar happiness to play in a scene with such as top their parts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good casting—pairing actors whose abilities complement or 'top' each other—raises the quality of scenes; directors should assemble casts to create productive contrasts and mutual elevation of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value actor-specific comic talents (physical/comic specialization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise of Mr. Bullock: 'a peculiar talent of looking like a fool, and therefore excellently well qualified for the part of Biskett... I cannot indeed sufficiently admire his way of bearing a beating... with such a natural air and propriety of folly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and exploit performers' special gifts (e.g., physical comedy, ability to take stage violence convincingly); such talents materially affect audience delight and comedic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of dramatic modes produce different pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between enjoying 'those excellent players... with a different sort of delight, than that which I receive from those grave scenes of Brutus and Cassius, or Antony and Ventidius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that low comedy and grave tragedy satisfy different aesthetic appetites; critics and producers should value both genres for their distinct effects rather than ranking one universally superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision and vivid single-line characterization in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Example from Sallust: a single sentence giving 'a lively impression of his whole life and actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly effective writing can convey a character's entire life and temperament in one well-chosen sentence; favor concentrated, vivid phrasing that leaves a strong impression with brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of low life may be 'just' and witty if well-handled
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The whole comedy is very just, and the low part of human life represented with much humour and wit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depicting lower strata or 'low' human behaviour need not be vulgar if treated with wit and justice; ethical representation and comic skill can make low life instructive and entertaining rather than merely degrading.
